title: Russell shares emotional reflection on 2026 in candid post
excerpt:
George Russell has opened up about the challenges of his 2026 campaign in an emotional social media post, admitting that the season has been one of the toughest of his career following Mercedes team mate Kimi Antonelli's World Championship triumph.

Russell took to Instagram on Monday to reflect on a year that had began with title ambitions but has since been marked by reliability issues and inconsistent performances, with the Briton acknowledging that he has struggled to rediscover his best form.

The post came a day after Antonelli secured his maiden Drivers' Championship at the Mexico City Grand Prix, becoming the youngest World Champion in Formula 1 history after finishing third behind Red Bull’s Max Verstappen and Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton.

Russell, meanwhile, endured another frustrating afternoon at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez, finishing sixth after a power deployment issue on the opening lap cost him several positions, while a subsequent collision with Isack Hadjar resulted in a 10-second time penalty.

Reflecting on his season, Russell wrote: "Now feels like a pretty suitable moment to speak from the heart.

"This season started off exactly how I had hoped but it very quickly unravelled with tough luck and poor performances. It’s been the first proper season of my career where I’ve had more bad days than good.

"Has it been tough to deal with? Yes, very. Has it been tough to pick myself up week in, week out? Yes, very. Confusion at times? Often. All I know is that I’ve given it my all and 2026 was not meant to be my year."

Russell began the campaign strongly with victory at the season-opening Australian Grand Prix, but his championship challenge gradually faded as Antonelli established himself at the front of the field.

Despite victories in Austria and Azerbaijan, Russell has struggled to consistently extract the maximum performance from Mercedes' W17, with Team Principal Toto Wolff pointing to the car's narrow operating window as a contributing factor. His difficulties continued in Mexico City, where a power deployment issue compromised his race after narrowly missing out on pole position.

Following the Grand Prix, Wolff admitted that Russell was "distraught" about the outcome, praising the Briton for congratulating Antonelli despite his own disappointment.

In his Instagram message, Russell again paid tribute to his team mate, writing: "I want to sincerely congratulate Kimi on what has been an absolutely incredible season. You truly deserve the Championship."

He also acknowledged Mercedes' return to the front of the grid under the new regulations, thanking those involved in developing the championship-winning package.

"Thank you to the team for producing the best car and power unit this season; it’s been inspiring to see everyone coming together over four tough years to bring Mercedes back to the top," he added.

With four rounds remaining in the 2026 campaign, Russell is now looking to finish the season strongly before turning his attention to next year, when he and Antonelli are set to continue as Mercedes team mates.

He continued: "Now, all I can promise is that for the rest of this season, and into the next one, I will be giving my absolute all to rediscover the performance I have been capable of producing for the majority of my career and fingers crossed a little bit of luck returns. Thanks for all the support."

title: Antonelli reveals race number he will use to defend title in 2027
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli has revealed what race number he will use to defend his Formula 1 drivers' title in 2027, having become World Champion in the Mexico City Grand Prix.

The Italian became the youngest driver to clinch the F1 title at the age of just 20 after finishing third during Sunday's 71-lap race at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez.

Antonelli took nine wins this year on his way to the title during his sophomore season, and only failed to reach the podium in three races.

Now that Antonelli has clinched the title, the Mercedes driver has a first-time decision to make – what race number he will use to defend his crown in 2027?

Since 2014, drivers have been able to pick their own race numbers, with the number 1 reserved only for the current champion to use.

Previously, Lewis Hamilton continued to use number 44 when winning his six titles for Mercedes, while Max Verstappen and more recently Lando Norris this season decided to use the number 1 after their title-winning campaigns.

Antonelli currently uses 12, the same number used by his idol Ayrton Senna when the Brazilian claimed the first of three titles with McLaren in 1988.

When asked post-race in Mexico what Antonelli would do for 2027, the new champion admitted the number 12 held even more special significance now.

"I think I'll stay with number 12," he said. "I'll stay with number 12 because, obviously, it's a very special number for me.

"But also it's a way for me to stay grounded, to stay humble, and I feel like by keeping number 12 it allows me to have a new point where to start and build on everything again and try to improve.

"And also, to be honest, I'm very superstitious, and number 1 has never been a good number for me. Whenever I put it, it went extremely badly. So one more reason to stay with number 12. But, yeah, I will stay with number 12."

title: Hirakawa assesses 'dream' F1 debut in Mexico City
excerpt:
Ryo Hirakawa's Formula 1 debut "was my dream" after the Japanese driver finished the Mexico City Grand Prix, eventually being promoted into the points.

Hirakawa was a late call-up to the Haas team, replacing Esteban Ocon at the American outfit on Saturday morning, but having already taken part in Free Practice 1 as a designated 'rookie' driver.

With another hour of practice under his belt, the 32-year-old eventually qualified P19 before starting his maiden Grand Prix from a spot higher on the grid after a penalty for Liam Lawson.

Hirakawa circulated in the midfield battle for much of the 71-lap race at Autodromo Hermanos Rodríguez on Sunday, eventually finishing P13 on the road, with seeing the chequered flag his ultimate goal.

But things became even better post-race, as Hirakawa joined an exclusive club of drivers to score points on their F1 debuts after time penalties for Oscar Piastri and the two Alpines of Franco Colapinto and Pierre Gasly promoted him to P10.

"Was a lot of things to do, especially the start and lap one, it was not easy," said Hirakawa before being promoted into the points.

"Especially here going to Turn 1 is so long you think about a lot of braking points, the cars side by side, in front, behind. So I think the start I took too much margin because I really wanted to finish the race because I want to learn. But it is what it is.

"After that I was trying to learn from the others what they are doing. Maybe the first stint was really tough, we didn't have the pace but I learnt a lot. After the Safety Car with the C5 [tyre], then I had more confidence and passed two cars. I'm happy to finish like that."

Haas are yet to confirm their driver line-up for this coming weekend in Brazil, with Hirakawa originally scheduled to compete for Toyota in the World Endurance Championship, where the title remains up for grabs.

Looking to the future, Hirakawa admitted he just had to savour the moment in Mexico for what might prove to be his only F1 start.

"I think I just need to taste this moment. I'm really happy, today was my dream," he said. "Just enjoy this moment and see what we can do."

title: Antonelli's incredible journey to his maiden F1 title
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli has made history by clinching his maiden World Championship, the Mercedes racer becoming the youngest-ever driver to take the crown after embarking on a stunning sophomore campaign. F1.com charts the journey of his triumphant 2026 season, from an initial setback through to his incredible run of victories…

Round 1, Australia – Bouncing back from an early crash

The season did not necessarily start in perfect fashion for Antonelli, with the youngster suffering a heavy crash in Free Practice 3 at the Australian Grand Prix. He quickly bounced back, however, by claiming P2 on the grid, which he converted into the same position come race day, helping Mercedes to secure a 1-2 finish alongside team mate George Russell.

Round 2, China – Converting first pole into maiden win

One week later in Shanghai, the tables turned at Mercedes. While Russell took another win in the Sprint, it was Antonelli who scored his maiden pole position – making him F1’s youngest-ever polesitter – before storming to his debut victory on Sunday.

Round 3, Japan – Becoming the youngest-ever championship leader

Antonelli’s impressive run of form continued at the Japanese Grand Prix, with another pole position and win resulting in the Italian climbing to the top of the drivers’ standings – a feat that saw him become the youngest driver to ever head the championship at 19 years, seven months and four days old.

Round 4, Miami – Making history with another win

Next time out in Miami, Antonelli dropped backwards in the Sprint, picking up a penalty for track limits en route to a P6 finish. Once again, however, the youngster recovered by seizing pole position and resisting pressure from a chasing Lando Norris to take another victory, making him the first driver in history to convert their first three poles into wins.

Round 5, Canada – Another win amid heartbreak for Russell

The Mercedes intra-team battle turned up a notch in Montreal, with Russell beating Antonelli after a fierce fight for the lead during the Sprint. Russell went on to secure pole for the Grand Prix, where the team mates resumed their thrilling scrap on track – but the duel came to an early end when Russell was forced to retire due to a power unit issue, resulting in Antonelli’s championship lead increasing to 43 points.

The records Antonelli has broken on his way to maiden title

Round 6, Monaco – Triumphing around the streets of Monte Carlo

Winning the Monaco Grand Prix is a feat that most drivers dream of achieving, and Antonelli boosted his chances of reaching the milestone by adding another pole position to his tally during an exciting Qualifying. The title leader kept his cool to win an eventful race, while penalties for Russell saw the British driver leave the event with no points.

Round 7, Barcelona – Title lead cut down after dramatic retirement

After climbing up to P2 during the latter stages of the Barcelona-Catalunya Grand Prix – following a close battle with Russell – Antonelli’s race came to a sudden end when he was forced to pull off track with a mechanical issue. The Italian admitted that his first retirement of the campaign had left him feeling “a bit empty”.

Round 8, Austria – Another boost for Russell in championship fight

The momentum again looked to be with Russell as F1 returned to Austria, with the Briton converting pole position into a victory. Antonelli had to settle for P3 behind the Red Bull of Max Verstappen, meaning that his championship lead now stood at 40 points.

Round 9, Great Britain – Sprint victory followed by a challenging race

Antonelli got back to winning ways at Silverstone by triumphing in the Sprint for the first time, having overtaken polesitter Lewis Hamilton on Lap 8. Race day was not quite so straightforward, however, with the youngster dropping backwards through the field due to a left front wheel shield failure. A penalty for track limits ultimately left him in P16 – a result that reduced his advantage in the standings down further to 25 points.

Round 10, Belgium – Return to the top step as title lead increases

Two weeks later in Belgium, Antonelli bounced back with his sixth pole of the season and a commanding victory on race day. Russell, meanwhile, found himself out of the running early on following Lap 1 contact with Hamilton, meaning that Antonelli now held a 45-point lead in the title fight.

Round 11, Hungary – Extending his lead despite challenges

After his pole and victory at Spa, Hungary proved to be a more challenging weekend for Antonelli and Mercedes – the Italian having to settle for P4 in Qualifying before being demoted to seventh on the grid for a yellow flag infringement. A different strategy and late-race Virtual Safety Car (when some rivals pitted again) brought him into podium contention, though, and he came away with P3 and an extended title lead.

'Unbelievable' - The F1 grid praise new champion Antonelli

Round 12, Netherlands – Strong starts “save” Antonelli’s race

When the Zandvoort Sprint weekend began, Russell appeared to have the upper hand in the Mercedes intra-team battle – the Briton taking P1 on Saturday, and Antonelli settling for fourth. However, in the Grand Prix itself, Antonelli launched past his team mate from the second row and then challenged Norris for the lead, before finishing runner-up to the McLaren man via a tough final stint on hard tyres.

Round 13, Italy – A comeback drive for the ages

Antonelli headed into his home Grand Prix weekend knowing that he would be starting from the back of the grid due to an engine-related penalty. What followed was an epic recovery drive that will no doubt go down as one of his finest performances in the sport. Starting from 19th, he was up to 14th by the end of the first lap and 12th after the second lap, before charging his way through the points-paying positions – eventually passing team mate Russell for a memorable win.

Round 14, Spain – Capitalising on Norris’ VSC misfortune

Antonelli was second-best to Norris in Qualifying at the all-new Madring, and it looked as though the McLaren driver would convert his pole into victory on race day with a strong start. However, an early Virtual Safety Car – coming out just at the wrong time for Norris – handed the lead to Antonelli, who controlled the remainder of the encounter to make it back-to-back wins.

Round 15, Azerbaijan – A tricky weekend on Baku’s streets

Antonelli faced a couple of major challenges when the Azerbaijan Grand Prix got underway, having lost valuable track time in practice due to technical problems and then crashing in the Q1 phase of Qualifying. While he recovered from 16th to fifth, Russell dominated proceedings, and Antonelli admitted afterwards that it represented “the worst weekend of the season for me”.

Round 16, Bahrain in Malaysia – Taking a huge step towards the title

The tables would turn once more next time out at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, which tested the drivers with rough tarmac and mixed weather conditions. As a dramatic wet/dry race drew to a close, Russell dramatically retired with an engine failure, giving Antonelli a clear run to second place – and another massive boost in terms of the championship situation.

Round 17, Singapore – Making his dream a mathematical possibility

Although Antonelli reported struggling with Mercedes' "very difficult" upgraded car during the early stages of the Singapore Grand Prix weekend, it didn't seem to show too much in his results. He finished fourth in the Sprint before improving to the podium on race day, and with Russell settling for a hard-fought P9, the Italian set himself up for a potential title win at the next round.

Antonelli's dad reflects on son's 'important' title triumph

Round 18, United States – Dominant victory edges him even closer

Arriving at the Circuit of The Americas with a 102-point lead over his team mate, Antonelli needed three things to go his way: one more race win, Russell to finish ninth or below, and Hamilton to place outside of the top four. He delivered on his side, converting what Toto Wolff described as a "miracle lap" in Qualifying to a supreme victory. Everything from his launch to tyre management and strategy was close to flawless, but both of his nearest rivals in the standings wound up just one position higher than he required, delaying what now seemed inevitable for one more week.

Round 19, Mexico City – Third on track, first in the history books

He had executed a champion's drive in Austin, so all that separated Antonelli from his record-breaking maiden title was a P9 finish in Mexico City. For the racer who had only missed out on the podium at three Grands Prix, that didn't sound like too big an ask. While he unsurprisingly felt "more tense than usual" before lining up in the P4 grid slot, he delivered the kind of level-headed performance he's grown into this season and snatched third place from Charles Leclerc. The subsequent podium celebration won't be forgotten any time soon, with the Italian hoisted onto the shoulders of two of the sport's most successful racers on the podium in Verstappen and Hamilton.

title: Bonnington names Antonelli’s top three races in title year
excerpt:
Pete Bonnington has selected his favourite three races that set Kimi Antonelli on the path towards becoming the 2026 World Champion, praising the Italian for his “mind-blowing” achievement.

Head of Race Engineering Bonnington – or ‘Bono’ – is no stranger to title success, having acted as Lewis Hamilton’s race engineer during his incredibly fruitful stint at Mercedes that saw him triumph six times between 2014 and 2020.

Once Hamilton departed the team for the 2025 season, Bonnington continued in his role for rookie Antonelli, guiding him through a challenging campaign before the now 20-year-old began to thrive under the new-for-2026 regulations.

After nine Grand Prix victories, Antonelli finished third at the Mexico City Grand Prix to secure the Drivers’ Championship, becoming the youngest to do so in the history of F1.

Asked which highlights stand out from the record-breaking season, Bonnington told F1 TV: “I think three stand out, and I think people will know what those three races are.

“For me, Monaco was just super special. It’s one of those races where if you can prove that to the rest of the grid, I think your peers respect you even more, and the way that he did it was just unbelievable.

“And then the Monza race… just wow. I remember turning around thinking, ‘oh, this is what the back of the grid looks like’, and then off we went. There was no stopping him.

“And then last weekend in Austin, that was a champion’s drive. It was the one-stop versus the two-stop. There’s the mental pressure in the car thinking, ‘I’m going to get caught, I’m going to get overtaken’, but no, he just kept his head down. He kept putting the lap times in and came out on top.

“Three drives of the year that really sealed that performance, but to be fair, other ones like Silverstone… without the failure, that would’ve been a really good result. Barcelona, we were looking good as well, so it’s that repeated performance that’s consistent. He can drive across a range of tracks, be it overheating, tyre warm-up, whatever.”

Bonnington is admired for his calm radio messages during races, but he and Antonelli have also garnered a reputation for pranking each other, with their off-track hijinks regularly shared across social media.

While it may not align with the high-stakes world of F1, the experienced race engineer insisted that having a more light-hearted relationship has been crucial to the Italian’s ability to remain focused and bounce back when he needs to.

“You can pick up a load of management books that will tell you any successful organisation has an element of fun in it, but he just does it naturally,” he explained. “It’s the way that he feels most comfortable, and it’s the way that he gets everyone else to feel comfortable.

“By having that element to the way that we work, it just sort of breaks down barriers so we can have open and honest conversations because we know at the end of the day we can still have a laugh and a joke. It’s a real big part.”

Elaborating on what Antonelli’s achievement means to him, he said: “Mind-blowing, I think is the word. It’s just been such an amazing journey with him. He’s really matured over this year and wow, he’s just grown into the World Champion that he is.

“It’s been a real fun year – the way that he’s brought that element into the team. He is the consummate professional and just such a talent.”

title: WRC champion returns after health issues derail single-seater dream
excerpt:
Two-time World Rally Champion Kalle Rovanperä will return to the WRC with GAZOO Racing TOYOTA in 2027 after health problems derailed his ambition of reaching Formula 1 through single-seater racing.

The 26-year-old left rallying at the end of 2025 to pursue a career in circuit racing, with plans to contest Japan's Super Formula championship in 2026 before progressing to Formula 2 in 2027.

However, the Finn's preparations were disrupted by benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV), an inner-ear condition causing dizziness and affecting balance and vision.

The condition forced him to abandon a Super Formula test at Suzuka in December 2025, before further illness interrupted his Formula Regional Oceania Trophy campaign.

Despite returning to Super Formula testing, Rovanperä withdrew from the championship in March following medical evaluations, having struggled with the physical demands of single-seater machinery.

He subsequently focused on his recovery before being cleared to resume driving, with Toyota offering him the opportunity to test its new-generation WRC car.

"I'm really happy to have the opportunity to compete in rallies with GAZOO Racing TOYOTA again next year. This team has always felt like family to me, and in a way I never really felt that I had left.

I'm enjoying having the chance to do some different things, but rallying has been a huge part of my life, and I naturally started to miss the driving after a while," said Rovanperä.

Rovanperä will reunite with co-driver Jonne Halttunen at GAZOO Racing TOYOTA, alongside returning 2019 champion Ott Tänak and Takamoto Katsuta.

Toyota will field two equal, competing teams under the new WRC regulations, with reigning champion Elfyn Evans joining Oliver Solberg and Sami Pajari at TOYOTA RACING.

The manufacturer enters 2027 following six consecutive manufacturers' titles, while Rovanperä returns seeking further success after winning the drivers' championships in 2022 and 2023.

"The main priority this year became my health once I was fit to drive again, the team offered me the opportunity to test the development car, and from there we started making plans for next season," Rovanperä added.

"It's an interesting time to come back, and while the new cars will be very different from what we had before, that makes it an exciting new challenge for me.

"The main thing will be to enjoy the driving and the competition, learn about the car, and see what we can do together."

title: Exclusive: Guenther Steiner calls on Italy to finally show Kimi Antonelli 'love' and 'respect'
excerpt:
Guenther Steiner believes Kimi Antonelli has yet to receive the recognition he deserves from their own country.

Antonelli became Italy's first F1 champion in 73 years, since Alberto Ascari, and the sport's youngest at 20 years and 68 days, after finishing third in the Mexico City Grand Prix.

Former Haas team principal Steiner, who was born in Merano and now runs his own MotoGP team, put that wait into perspective when discussing what the achievement would mean for Italian motorsport.

"Seventy-three years! It's a bloody long time!" said Steiner, speaking exclusively to RacingNews365. "If you put the number on there, it's unbelievable that it's taken this long.

"And what does it mean [for Italy]? It means a lot. But even though Italy has not had a driver as world champion for so long, they've had Ferrari, and they still have Ferrari, which is the national team."

Steiner pointed to Ferrari's grip on Italian motorsport culture as the reason Antonelli's title has not yet captured the national imagination in the way it might elsewhere.

"I think we need to wait to see what it does because I sometimes think that Kimi doesn't get the respect he deserves from the country," he said.

"Obviously, the country is used to cheering for Ferrari, and not for one of their drivers because they've not had one for so long, or at least at world championship level.

"I think that a lot of people need to get used to it because, for them, they just see the Scuderia, which is what they follow, and Kimi deserves a little bit more support from the people there."

Steiner drew a comparison with Jannik Sinner, the Italian tennis player who has become a mainstream national hero despite an understated public style that initially drew scrutiny from parts of the Italian press.

"I mean, Italy now has two big champions, Jannik Sinner and Kimi Antonelli," he said. "Jannik gets a lot of love from the country, and I hope that Kimi will now get the same love as well."

[Article continues below]

Antonelli's rise has been rapid. He joined Mercedes' junior programme in 2019, skipped Formula 3 entirely on his way through the junior categories, and was handed the seat vacated by Lewis Hamilton's move to Ferrari for 2025.

Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff has previously urged the Italian media to avoid heaping excessive pressure on the youngster or drawing premature comparisons to figures such as Ayrton Senna.

Steiner, though, was full of praise for how Antonelli has handled his rookie season, in particular going up against George Russell, a driver he was quick to point out is no pushover.

"Amazing!" said Steiner of Antonelli's overall achievement this year. "I think we all knew that he was pretty good from what we saw last year, but there are a lot of talented drivers now.

"But how he has taken to his role at Mercedes and beaten George, and George is a good driver. He's no slouch.

"To race the way he has for a 20-year-old, making very few mistakes, never appearing to be under stress, is fantastic.

"I think we all thought that maybe the second half of this season, the same would happen as last year at McLaren with Oscar [Piastri] and Lando [Norris]. But no, he kept his cool.

"And he's very calculating as well. If he knows that he cannot win, he gets the best out of it, which is normally a podium.

"He's so very mature for a 20-year-old. It's nice to see that young people can be like him as well, as a person. He's a very good kid, which is nice to see from the outside."

title: Honda take blame and issue solemn vow after costly Aston Martin oversight
excerpt:
Honda has accepted responsibility for the double retirement that befell Aston Martin at the Mexico City Grand Prix, with trackside general manager and chief engineer Shintaro Orihara admitting the Japanese manufacturer underestimated the cooling demands of the high-altitude circuit.

Fernando Alonso's race at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez ended in a DNF, having already been compromised by power unit trouble in qualifying that restricted him to P17 on the grid.

Lance Stroll fared no better, affected by the same issue that struck his team-mate as they were both forced into retirement on Lap 5 of 71.

It capped a miserable weekend for the Silverstone-based outfit, whose power unit partnership with Honda has been troubled for much of the 2026 campaign.

Severe vibration issues damaged battery packs and curtailed pre-season running, while the engine has also lagged behind rival manufacturers on straight-line power through the year.

Orihara explained that Honda had anticipated some difficulty given the unique demands of racing nearly 2,250 metres above sea level, where thinner air reduces cooling efficiency and forces turbochargers to work harder to compress sufficient oxygen into the combustion chambers.

"We knew that with the special high-altitude circumstance of Mexico City, we would face some additional challenges compared to other racetracks for the cooling," Orihara conceded before admitting the scale of the problem caught Honda out.

"However, we found that our ERS cooling circuit was under heavier stress than anticipated, and this is why we had to stop the car in different sessions."

[Article continues below]

Hard lessons for 2027

The chief engineer revealed that the fault had shown no warning signs in earlier runs, only to resurface when it mattered most.

He added: "Despite completing a series of laps during the practice sessions, the issue occurred [in the race] and during qualifying..."

Orihara was explicit that Honda intends to use the setback as a building block for next year's redesigned power unit, with HRC understood to be targeting a two-phase overhaul ahead of the opening rounds of the 2027 season.

"At each race this year, we need to learn for 2027, even the hard lessons," he said. "We have a lot of data that we can bring back to this circuit next year, including on the turbo lag, and we will work on the solutions."

title: Toto Wolff reveals Mercedes shocking sponsor backlash after signing Kimi Antonelli
excerpt:
Toto Wolff has said that multiple sponsors ended their relationship with Mercedes after the signing of newly crowned F1 drivers' champion Kimi Antonelli.

Toto Wolff has revealed that two sponsors ended their affiliation with Mercedes over the signing of Kimi Antonelli ahead of the 2025 F1 season.

Antonelli became Formula 1's youngest drivers' champion at the Mexico City Grand Prix, and the boss of the Brackley-based squad was keen to highlight the return on investment the 20-year-old has represented for team partners.

Not only did Antonelli beat Sebastian Vettel's record by over three years, but he also became the first Italian to win the title in 73 years.

Like Jacques Villeneuve and Lewis Hamilton, in 1997 and 2008, respectively, he is just the third driver in F1's modern era to clinch the crown in his second campaign.

Reflecting on the momentous achievement at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez, Wolff shared how quickly he realised the time was right for Antonelli to ascend to F1 once Hamilton opted to leave for Ferrari.

"We have to pinch ourselves because it seems like yesterday he was 11 years old in a garage in junior karting and it goes so fast," Wolff told Sky Sports F1. "He wins the junior formulas, then a difficult year in F2 and that's already where people start outside started to doubt.

"Then when Lewis told me he was going to Ferrari, it was my immediate reaction that we’ve got to put him in the car. But people doubted. We had two sponsors leaving us because of that, because of 'who is this kid?'

"There were others who stayed with us until today. Some are here that reaped the full reward."

Wolff: Antonelli was a 'calculated risk, not a real risk'

Antonelli endured a trying debut season in F1. Although he frequently displayed the pace and potential that earned him the seat alongside team-mate George Russell, he suffered through considerable low points, including his torrid run of results once the paddock reached Europe.

"And then the difficult year and people said again, he shouldn't even be in Formula 1, or he should be at a smaller team," Wolff added. "Over nine races [in Europe], no points, the tears in Spa and then this.

"I'm just so proud for the team that all of them continue to trust him and he delivered."

Expanding on how instantly he knew he wanted Antonelli to graduate to not only F1, but to the works Mercedes team, Wolff insisted it was never an unmitigated risk.

"It was instinctive. Lewis left. I called Bradley [Lord, deputy team principal] and said, 'Kimi is in the car next year'," he explained. "We knew the data, so it kind of felt like the right thing to do. I think it was always a calculated risk, not a real risk."

title: Lewis Hamilton takes clear stance in 'incredibly frustrating' social media statement
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton has taken to social media to further address the first-lap fight with Ferrari team-mate Charles Leclerc in Mexico — and to congratulate Kimi Antonelli for winning the F1 drivers' championship.

Lewis Hamilton has doubled down on his post-Mexico City Grand Prix remarks, taking to social media to express how "incredibly frustrating" his clash with Charles Leclerc was.

Hamilton reiterated his view that the team and the Ferrari fans deserve more than the Scuderia's two drivers ultimately costing themselves the opportunity to fight for victory.

On the first lap at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez, the seven-time F1 drivers' champion and Leclerc emerged from the opening sequence of corners leading.

However, the Monegasque driver attacked into Turn 4, with Hamilton attempting in vain to defend the position. Both ran wide and off the track. The former cut the corner, and the latter lost momentum.

The confluence of events allowed Max Verstappen to grab second from Hamilton, preventing Leclerc from giving the position back and all but ensuring he received a five-second time penalty, which handed the Dutchman the lead at the pit stop phase.

The Briton went on to take the chequered flag in second, behind the Red Bull driver. The old adversaries shared the podium with Kimi Antonelli, who was crowned F1's youngest drivers' champion, an experience Hamilton relished.

"Let me start with a huge congratulations to the new champion, Kimi Antonelli," he wrote on social media whilst tagging the new F1 drivers' champion. "To have seen your journey so closely and share to be there celebrating with you, was a highlight of my year.

"So well deserved and a record that will stand for a long time. It was great to see your team at Mercedes celebrating with you. Enjoy this moment, keep your family close, keep your passion and your energy."

[Article continues below]

Hamilton: 'I can't pretend otherwise...'

Turning to the calamitous battle with his team-mate, which Ferrari boss Fred Vasseur argued underlined a "lack of respect" from his drivers, Hamilton insisted he and Leclerc must "grasp every opportunity" after another shot at winning slipped away.

"Our own weekend was one full of challenges. We had a lot thrown at us, but our mechanics and engineers did an incredible job," he said.

"We've grown so much together this year, and that progress has taken a huge effort from everyone on the track and back at the factory.

"That's why losing what could've been a win hurts so much. We need to grasp every opportunity we have, so it's incredibly frustrating, and I can't pretend otherwise."

Hamilton did not hold back in the comments he made following the 71-lap race, and he neither apologised nor claimed responsibility on social media for the unnecessary squandering of a golden chance for which Leclerc is broadly being seen as the catalyst.

The 106-time grand prix winner called for "honest" reflection and to "learn" from the mistakes in judgement that culminated in Verstappen taking victory.

"I know what goes into giving us that opportunity. The standard the team holds itself to, the standard I hold myself to, the standard the fans expect. Everyone deserves to see us at our best and win," the 41-year-old said.

"We're all here to race and want to win. Battling is necessary, but when that battle costs the team, we have to be honest about it and learn from it.

"We can push each other to the limit and still honour the responsibility to everyone who put us on that track.

"I'll keep giving everything I have. My belief in this team hasn't changed, and neither has my responsibility to help us get this right. Stick with us. I'm only just getting started with this team, and we have so much more to come."

title: Exclusive: Kimi Antonelli handed Max Verstappen verdict by Bernie Ecclestone: 'You'll see'
excerpt:
Max Verstappen is without a doubt a generational talent. Bernie Ecclestone is convinced Kimi Antonelli will follow in his footsteps.

Bernie Ecclestone believes Kimi Antonelli will "turn into another Max Verstappen" within two to three years after the Mercedes driver became Formula 1's youngest world champion at the Mexico City Grand Prix.

Antonelli sealed the title at 20 years and 68 days old, beating Sebastian Vettel's long-standing record by a remarkable three years, whilst he also became Italy's first title winner in 73 years.

Ecclestone, who ran F1 for 40 years before stepping down as chief executive in 2017, has seen more than one generation of champions up close. The 95-year-old now sees the same ingredients in Antonelli that carried Verstappen to four world titles.

"There are two people I once hoped would win the championship, one is Max, one is him," said Ecclestone, speaking exclusively to RacingNews365.

"Although I don't know him as well as I know Max, I think he will turn into another Max.

"He's got all that Max has got; he wants to win, and he will win no matter what. He's the same as Max in that he gets into the car with only one thought in his mind: winning the race."

The parenting difference between Antonelli and Verstappen

Ecclestone drew a contrast between how Verstappen and Antonelli were raised by their fathers. Jos Verstappen is known to have put his son through gruelling conditioning as a child, including running karting laps on slick tyres in freezing or wet conditions to sharpen his car control.

Marco Antonelli has taken a different route, leaning on his own team AKM Motorsport and his links with Kart Republic in his son's junior years while leaving the heavy lifting of career management to Mercedes' junior programme.

"Max, in his day [as a kid], his dad was a bit strict with him, but he made him wake up and get going," said Ecclestone.

"Whereas Kimi's dad seems to be the opposite, sympathises with him, and tries to keep him a little bit calm.

"But we haven't seen the best of him yet by a long way. I think we'll be surprised at how good he's going to be.

"You will see, he's going to turn into another Max in two to three years.

"He needs to have a few rough times to polish him up a little bit, and then watch out."

[Article continues below]

© XPB Images

Ecclestone - 'Life isn't that simple'

Asked how that polishing process might happen, Ecclestone pointed back to the Verstappen blueprint.

"The best thing to do is an awful lot of what Max's dad did to him, and make him understand that life isn't that simple," he said.

"You've got to accept the bad, as well as the good, and make sure the bad doesn't happen again."

Ecclestone also suggested Antonelli's age means his growth as both driver and champion is still only beginning.

"He's only just finished being a teenager, so it's going to take a little longer for him to grow into what he has just become, a world champion," he said.

"And for someone so young, he could easily eclipse all records, sure, sure, sure."

title: McLaren make Lando Norris 'eyes closed' joke as 'harsh' penalty deepens anger
excerpt:
It was another weekend of frustration for McLaren.

McLaren team principal Andrea Stella believes Lando Norris spent so long stuck behind rivals in the Mexico City Grand Prix that he could now draw their cars from memory.

Stella was also left disenchanted by a post-race penalty for Oscar Piastri that relegated the Australian driver out of the points, to add salt to the wounds of a disappointing weekend.

Norris finished fifth at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez after failing to find a way past George Russell's Mercedes initially, and then Charles Leclerc's Ferrari despite running in their wake for long stretches.

Piastri, who had endured a difficult qualifying, fought back from 12th on the grid to cross the line in seventh.

The stewards, however, handed him a 10-second time penalty after ruling he had caused a Turn 1 collision with Arvid Lindblad late in the race, concluding the McLaren driver was never fully alongside the VCARB 03 and had no right to the corner. The penalty dropped Piastri to 15th.

Speaking after the race, Stella said McLaren had the pace and "potential to finish on the podium".

"Unfortunately, we paid the price for both our drivers' starting grid positions and the limitations imposed by the technical regulations, which make overtaking practically impossible on a track like this," said Stella.

"With all the time Lando spent in the slipstream, first behind Russell and then behind Leclerc, I think he could now draw the rear of their cars with his eyes closed!

"Furthermore, the harsh penalty Oscar received for the contact with Lindblad cost us further valuable points: a real shame because Oscar had staged a good comeback."

Stella - 'We'll have to be perfect'

McLaren's result leaves the team fourth in the constructors' standings battle, 17 points behind Red Bull after Verstappen's victory.

Stella has confirmed the team is now targeting this weekend's Brazilian Grand Prix to close the margin, with upgrades planned.

"In our battle with Red Bull for third place, we could only limit the damage after a qualifying session that had put us in a difficult position," said Stella.

"We have points to make up, but I believe that with the pace we showed and the upgrades coming to Brazil, we have every chance of achieving at least that target.

"To do so, however, we'll have to be perfect as a team, in every respect."

© XPB Images

Antonelli triumph 'truly exceptional'

Stella also praised fellow Italian Kimi Antonelli after the 20-year-old became the youngest champion in F1 history after finishing third in the race, and the first from their country in an astonishing 73 years.

"On behalf of the whole team, I would like to congratulate Kimi and Mercedes on a truly historic achievement," said Stella.

"Becoming the youngest world champion in the history of Formula 1 in just his second season is something extraordinary.

"For Italian motor racing, Kimi now joins an exclusive group alongside legendary names, Alberto Ascari and Giuseppe Farina, who have inspired entire generations of Italian fans.

"His incredible consistency, his reliability and the remarkable progress he has made over the past year have made this triumph truly exceptional."

title: Kimi Antonelli Mercedes ally makes key admission: 'But it was so rough'
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli's race engineer Peter Bonnington has admitted he did not envisage the Mercedes driver would reach the heights of F1 drivers' champion so early in his career.

Antonelli — who 'Bono', as he is affectionately known, described as a "diamond in the rough" when their partnership began — became Formula 1's youngest champion by finishing third at the Mexico City Grand Prix.

In doing so, he beat Sebastian Vettel's record by over three years, becoming the first Italian to be crowned in 73 seasons and just the third driver in contemporary F1 to win the title in their second campaign, after Jacques Villeneuve and Lewis Hamilton.

Whilst Antonelli now finds himself in exalted company, Bonnington expressed how far the 20-year-old has come in only a couple of years.

"I think 'diamond in the rough' is exactly the thing that I saw initially... in TPC [testing of previous cars], there was a diamond in the rough, but it was so rough," Bonnington told Sky Sports F1.

The young Italian embarked on a 9,000- to 10,000-kilometre testing programme ahead of his F1 debut, which he dovetailed with just a single season in Formula 2, having skipped FIA Formula 3 altogether.

"Trying to prove it in an F2 car is okay, but I think you need to go to the next level to experience the power of the downforce to see whether you can make that step," Bonnington added, before revealing his surprise at how quickly Antonelli has scaled the mountain of conquering F1.

"But he really did that, and from there, 'Okay, [he's a ]diamond in the rough, but he's going to need a lot of work.' I didn't think it would be this quick. I thought it was going to take us a few years."

[Article continues below]

Defying expectations

Heading into the F1 season, Antonelli was widely anticipated to play second fiddle to George Russell as he continued his development.

However, it soon became apparent that he had meshed better with the W17 and the new regulations, becoming the hallmark of consistency whilst his team-mate faltered.

It defied all expectations, including Bonnington's, who did not start to believe the title could be Antonelli's until his driver was concluding the five-round winning streak that ultimately defined his campaign.

"Obviously, we've got such a great team-mate with George, such a strong driver, and we'll be able to learn off him," Bonnington said.

"But coming into this year, some exceptional performances, and I think it was just as we were getting into Europe, I thought, 'Well, maybe [we can win the title], but let's just keep it on the down low, and we'll just crack on'."

title: Lewis Hamilton demands Ferrari find solutions after latest mess with Charles Leclerc
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton was far from impressed with how the intra-Ferrari squabble with Charles Leclerc panned out on the first lap of the Mexico City Grand Prix.

Lewis Hamilton has called on Ferrari to "figure out" how to avoid throwing away strong results through wheel-to-wheel battles with Charles Leclerc.

Not for the first time this F1 season, Hamilton and Leclerc have cost themselves dearly by fighting each other on the first lap.

This time, they stood a good chance of taking a third victory of the campaign, and a one-two finish at the Mexico City Grand Prix

The Ferrari team-mates emerged from Turn 1 in first and second at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez, but Leclerc's eagerness to attack saw them both run wide at Turn 4. Hamilton dropped to third, behind Max Verstappen.

The Monegasque driver was handed a race-defining five-second time penalty for going off track and gaining an advantage, for what was ultimately a needless risk at that stage of the grand prix.

It follows a similar, costly incident at Monza, in front of the adoring Tifosi, where Leclerc pushed the seven-time F1 driver's champion off at the second corner, with only Pierre Gasly and George Russell ahead.

Reflecting on a result that slipped through the Scuderia's fingers, Hamilton, who finished second with Leclerc fourth, told Sky Sports F1: "I gave it everything.

"Unfortunately, the race was lost in the first few corners, and it's a shame because we could have easily finished first and second in this race if we worked together as a team."

Driver

Lewis Hamilton

British

44

Hamilton was keen to stress that he and Leclerc do not race solely for themselves, and that they represent a wider team, making squandering such opportunities unacceptable; something a furious Fred Vasseur also said.

The 41-year-old vented his frustration over team radio during the race, including highlighting that such incidents had been covered in the drivers' briefing, where it was agreed positions would be given back in such scenarios, which Leclerc could not do once Verstappen got by.

Asked whether there was a discussion at Ferrari prior to the race about being more strategic during the opening lap, Hamilton replied: "We didn't sit down and talk before.

"Again, it's something I mentioned in the past, but it's all fair and well racing against your team-mate as long as it's not to the detriment of the team's points and the team's opportunity of getting the result.

"At the end of the day, the team has to come first, and today we lost the win for the team; today we lost points, I lost second in the championship, and that's a real shame.

"It affects so many people back at the factory. Luckily we still got points so we can hold onto second in the constructors', but it impacts the people that put in all the hard work, and the Tifosi. So it wasn't good."

Whilst there were no conversations at Ferrari before the race, Hamilton insisted they needed to happen afterwards, maintaining the team would address the situation.

"It definitely needs some discussions for sure, but we'll take it offline and figure out what we can do," he added.

title: George Russell issues statement 'from the heart' after 'catastrophic' title defeat
excerpt:
George Russell has issued a statement after his title defeat to Kimi Antonelli.

George Russell has released his first public comments since Kimi Antonelli claimed the Formula 1 drivers' title in Mexico City.

After the Italian finished third to become the youngest F1 champion, Russell quickly left the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez without talking to the media, something which earned Mercedes a €5,000 fine.

Russell had finished sixth after incurring a 10-second time penalty for a collision on the opening lap with Isack Hadjar after starting on the front-row - but where a deployment issue on the run to Turn 1 had dropped him down the order.

Post-race, Mercedes boss Toto Wolff labelled the result as a "catastrophic moment" for the Briton, who was "distraught."

Now, nearly 24 hours after the end of the race, Russell has taken to social media.

In a lengthy statement on Instagram, Russell described how his season had "quickly unravelled" after a dominant pole and win in the season-opener in Australia - as he vowed to "rediscover the performance I've been capable of producing for the majority of my career."

[Read the full statement below]

"Now feels like a pretty suitable moment to speak from the heart.

"This season started off exactly how I had hoped but it very quickly unravelled with tough luck and poor performances.

"It’s been the first proper season of my career where I’ve had more bad days than good. Has it been tough to deal with? Yes, very.

"Has it been tough to pick myself up week in, week out? Yes, very. Confusion at times? Often. All I know is that I’ve given it my all and 2026 was not meant to be my year.

"I want to sincerely congratulate Kimi on what has been an absolutely incredible season. You truly deserve the Championship.

"Thank you to the team for producing the best car and power unit this season; it’s been inspiring to see everyone coming together over four tough years to bring Mercedes back to the top.

"Now, all I can promise is that for the rest of this season, and into the next one, I will be giving my absolute all to rediscover the performance I have been capable of producing for the majority of my career and fingers crossed a little bit of luck returns.

"Thanks for all the support."

title: Liam Lawson lands 'done everything' praise as F1 future uncertainty grows
excerpt:
Racing Bulls CEO Peter Bayer has acknowledged that Liam Lawson has "done everything" he can to prove himself within the team.

Lawson has enjoyed a successful campaign this year and has been a regular finisher inside the points, with 83 to his name after the Mexico City Grand Prix.

The New Zealander is on course to end the campaign ninth in the drivers' championship, the first position outside the drivers from the leading teams.

However, he has not yet secured a drive on the 2027 F1 grid and is believed to be facing competition from Red Bull junior Nikola Tsolov.

While Lawson has impressed, Bayer insisted that Racing Bulls' core goal is to assess fresh talent when it becomes available.

"He has certainly done everything to prove himself," Bayer told ORF. "That's also the general consensus in the paddock.

"As a team that plays a leading role in developing new Formula 1 talent, it's our job to continually bring new drivers into the series.

"We've already helped a total of 22 drivers make it to Formula 1, including Sebastian Vettel and Max Verstappen.

"That's why I also say that the decision will ultimately rest with Alan. He'll make the right choice for the team."

Bayer issues praise to challenger Tsolov

Tsolov is currently fighting for the Formula 2 title and sits seven points down on leader Rafael Camara with two rounds to go.

The Bulgarian made his F1 weekend debut last weekend in Mexico, taking part in FP1 as part of the mandatory rookie outings teams must provide.

Tsolov ended the session in 12th, drawing praise from Bayer.

"Nikola's stint on Friday was really great. It was his first time in this car, and he integrated perfectly into the team.

"As for the decision regarding next year's driver lineup, that decision rests with Alan.

"He'll make a decision and announce it when he thinks the time is right."

title: George Russell told to get 'nasty' as Liam Lawson sabotage claims denied — International Media reacts
excerpt:
Find out how media from around the world reacted to the 2026 F1 Mexico City Grand Prix, held at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez.

Kimi Antonelli became the youngest world champion in Formula 1 history at the Mexico City Grand Prix, as Max Verstappen claimed a dramatic victory at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez.

The Mercedes driver finished third to secure his maiden title at just 20 years and 68 days old, breaking Sebastian Vettel's long-standing record and becoming the first Italian to win the drivers' championship since Alberto Ascari in 1953.

Verstappen held off Lewis Hamilton by just 0.799 seconds to secure his third victory of the season, with Antonelli completing the podium.

There was plenty of controversy throughout the race, particularly at Ferrari, where Hamilton and Charles Leclerc clashed on the opening lap.

Leclerc was handed a five-second penalty for leaving the track and gaining an advantage, while George Russell also received a penalty following contact with Isack Hadjar.

A heavy crash for Valtteri Bottas subsequently brought out the red flags, adding another twist to an eventful afternoon in Mexico.

With Antonelli now officially crowned world champion, attention has turned to the extraordinary investment Mercedes made in the Italian's development, the growing tensions at Ferrari and the ongoing uncertainty surrounding Liam Lawson's future.

Here's how the international media reacted to the Mexico City Grand Prix, the 19th round of the 2026 F1 season.

🇬🇧 The Telegraph – Antonelli's victory will break Russell unless he gets nasty

The Telegraph examines the potentially damaging consequences of Antonelli's championship triumph for Mercedes team-mate George Russell, who has been comprehensively overshadowed by the young Italian throughout 2026.

Having entered the season as the more experienced driver and a potential title favourite, Russell now faces the prospect of playing second fiddle to Formula 1's youngest world champion.

The newspaper suggests that Russell may need to adopt a more ruthless approach if he is to reassert himself within Mercedes, particularly as Antonelli's success threatens to establish a new hierarchy at the team.

With the Italian already achieving what Russell has spent years pursuing, the psychological challenge facing the Briton could prove just as significant as the battle on track.

🇳🇱 De Telegraaf – Lewis Hamilton furious with Charles Leclerc and delivers harsh Ferrari criticism: 'It's clear something has to change'

De Telegraaf focuses on Hamilton's frustration with Ferrari following a controversial opening-lap battle with team-mate Leclerc in Mexico City.

The seven-time world champion was unhappy after Leclerc cut across the grass while attempting to overtake him, with the incident allowing Verstappen to capitalise and ultimately costing Ferrari a potential victory.

Although Leclerc received a five-second penalty, Hamilton remained critical of the team's handling of the situation and suggested changes were necessary to prevent similar incidents.

The Dutch publication highlights the growing tension within Ferrari, with Hamilton's second-place finish doing little to disguise his disappointment at another missed opportunity for the Scuderia.

🇮🇹 Gazzetta dello Sport – How much has Antonelli cost Mercedes? The figures behind Wolff's project

Gazzetta dello Sport examines the extraordinary investment Mercedes made in Antonelli's development, revealing that the team spent more than €10 million nurturing the Italian's talent over nine years.

Toto Wolff explained that Mercedes identified Antonelli when he was just 11 years old and continued supporting him despite a difficult rookie campaign in 2025, when some rival teams questioned whether he deserved a place in Formula 1.

The Austrian recalled how Antonelli was reduced to tears following a particularly challenging race at Spa, but insisted the team's faith in him never wavered.

Gazzetta consequently presents his historic championship triumph as the culmination of a long-term project built on financial commitment, patience and an unwavering belief in his potential.

🇫🇷 L'Équipe – Ferrari struggling to accept Mexico GP result: 'It's difficult to throw away a victory like that'

L'Équipe highlights Ferrari's bitter disappointment after a race in which the Italian team appeared capable of securing victory but ultimately had to settle for second and fourth.

Hamilton started from pole position, but his opening-lap battle with Leclerc compromised both drivers and allowed Verstappen to move into contention for the lead.

The French publication focuses on Ferrari's frustration at squandering a golden opportunity, with the team's internal rivalry and subsequent strategic decisions contributing to its failure to convert strong qualifying pace into victory.

Although Hamilton pushed Verstappen to within eight-tenths of a second at the finish, the result left Ferrari reflecting on what might have been rather than celebrating a potentially significant win.

🇩🇪 Bild – The title-winning night in Formula 1: King Kimi was in tears on the final lap

Bild provides a behind-the-scenes account of Kimi Antonelli's emotional championship celebrations after the Mercedes driver became Formula 1's youngest world champion at the Mexico City Grand Prix.

The Italian revealed that he had been forced to slow down on the final lap as tears filled his eyes, before receiving congratulations from Lewis Hamilton and race winner Max Verstappen, who later lifted him onto their shoulders during the podium ceremony.

Antonelli subsequently celebrated with his family and Mercedes personnel, paying tribute to the team and those closest to him for helping him achieve his childhood dream.

Bild also highlights Toto Wolff's pride in his young protégé, with the Mercedes team principal insisting Antonelli had demonstrated that a driver did not need to be selfish to become world champion.

🇳🇿 NZ Herald – No, there is not a Racing Bulls conspiracy to sabotage Liam Lawson

The NZ Herald challenges suggestions that Racing Bulls is deliberately undermining Lawson, arguing that the difficulties experienced by the New Zealander should not automatically be interpreted as evidence of a conspiracy.

The opinion piece addresses the growing speculation surrounding Lawson's treatment within the Red Bull organisation, particularly as uncertainty continues over his long-term future with the team.

Rather than attributing disappointing results or questionable decisions to deliberate interference, the publication urges a more measured assessment of the challenges facing both driver and team.

Lawson's points finish in Mexico provides another reminder of his capabilities, but the article suggests that conspiracy theories risk distracting from a more complicated sporting situation.

title: Toyota issues incredibly emotional letter after ‘unforgettable’ Hirakawa F1 debut
excerpt:
Ryo, congratulations on your F1 debut! And most of all, thank you. From the bottom of my heart. Ever since Toyota withdrew from F1 in 2009, there has been a feeling I have carried with me.

I believe every racing driver dreams of one day driving the fastest car in the world. I wanted to find a way to make that dream come true for our drivers. I wanted to see a Toyota driver race in F1 again.

That was a dream I had quietly held in my heart for 17 years. Through our partnership with Haas, we gradually created opportunities for our drivers to take on the challenge of F1, through testing and FP1 sessions.

And now, 17 years after 2009, that day has finally come. One of Toyota’s drivers has raced in a Formula 1 Grand Prix. And I could not be happier that it was Ryo Hirakawa.

When I last met Ryo, it was after he had faced a difficult outcome in his pursuit of a full-time race seat for the following season. At that time, Ryo promised me that he would never give up.

Drivers are reaching F1 at an increasingly young age. And I felt truly sorry that Ryo had to go through so many difficulties along the way.

I told him, "When you have to make a choice, choose the path that makes you happy. Choose what you really want to do." Even so, Ryo never stopped preparing.

He kept himself in the best possible condition, ready to deliver his very best whenever an opportunity might come along, even though nobody knew when that opportunity would arrive, or whether it would ever come at all.

He kept going without any guarantee that his efforts would be rewarded. That is why I am so happy to see him make his F1 debut.

After driving in FP1 on Friday, Ryo was suddenly called up the following morning to drive in FP3 and qualifying on Saturday, and then the race on Sunday. With very little time to prepare, he showed the pace to fight for a place in Q2, and in the race, he kept pushing right to the end.

The final result may not have been what he had hoped for. But seeing Ryo take on the world’s highest level of motorsport with such confidence and determination made me incredibly proud. When I saw Ryo line up on the F1 grid, I felt that one of my own dreams had finally come true, too.

Ryo, thank you for making my dream come true. I also want to express my heartfelt thanks to Gene Haas, Ayao Komatsu, and every engineer, mechanic and member of the TGR Haas F1 Team.

This day would not have been possible without your trust in Ryo, your support, and the tremendous effort of every single person in the team. It takes so many people working together to make one driver’s dream of racing in F1 come true.

To each and every one of you, thank you. Truly. My heartfelt thanks also go to Ryo’s family, who have supported him throughout his journey, to the fans who never stopped cheering for him, and to everyone else who has supported him along the way.

Ryo’s drive has brought dreams and inspiration to so many children. In endurance racing, Ryo has already reached the very top of the world. Now, I hope he can take the next steps in Formula racing, too. First, scoring points. Then, standing on the podium. I want all of us to cheer him on, together with the fans, one step at a time.

And one day, I hope to see a Japanese driver standing on the top step of an F1 podium. Nobody knows when the next opportunity will come. But after everything Ryo has endured, all the patience he has shown, and all the hard work he has put in while continuing to believe in his dream, I believe he will give us another reason to dream.

Gene, Ayao, and everyone at TGR Haas F1 Team, Let’s continue creating opportunities for our drivers to chase their dreams. Building cars and going racing are never things we can do alone. It is about people connecting, becoming friends and teammates, and chasing dreams together.

I want to keep racing forward with all of you, as one team. Ryo, thank you for giving us such an unforgettable moment. And thank you for making my dream come true, too!

title: Lewis Hamilton scolds Charles Leclerc 'do or die' mentality after latest clash
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton has scolded Charles Leclerc for his approach to wheel-to-wheel racing, suggesting his team-mate needs a mentality shift going forward.

The Ferrari duo were involved in an opening lap scrap for the lead of the race, with both running into Turn 4.

Leclerc was subsequently given a five-second time penalty for gaining an advantage off the track, which eventually handed the lead to Max Verstappen, who slipped ahead of Hamilton after the opening lap skirmish.

Hamilton stated after the race that he was "really pissed" with the situation, while Ferrari team boss Fred Vasseur accused both drivers of lacking respect.

It is not the first time this year Hamilton has felt aggrieved with his team-mate, as they also had an opening lap tussle at Monza that resulted in the seven-time champion losing several places.

Hamilton asserted that Leclerc's approach to racing is nothing new.

"Before I joined this team, when I was at Mercedes, I watched and witnessed the back-and-forth between Charles and Carlos several races," Hamilton told media including RacingNews365.

"They were battling so much that the person ahead just pulled away, and they had the pace to actually win."

[Article continues below]

Hamilton points to 'kamikaze' avoidance at Silverstone

Hamilton started the race from pole position, having achieved his first with Ferrari on Saturday in Mexico.

The incident between the duo severely hindered Ferrari's chances of a third win in 2026.

Hamilton called on his team-mate to look at his approach from Silverstone earlier this year, when he avoided a "kamikaze" move to strip Leclerc of a race win.

"It is one thing when that's happening in fourth and fifth, as opposed to first and second, and you lose the win," he said.

"That's significant. The guy is 28 years old, so I don't think it's an age thing. I think it's a mentality thing.

"It's like, 'Do or die. Either I win or none of us do', and it shouldn't be that.

"It should be us having, getting that one-two. As I said, it's still a good feeling.

"Silverstone, I could have gone all kamikaze on him and taken him off and lost us the win, but instead the one-two [sic] was there.

"For me, I'm happy for the team to have experienced that, but I'm hopeful we'll work towards a better place, a better working place, in the future."
